Otolaryngology · published research

Auditory neuropathy

In ouabain-injured gerbils, laser treatment lowered elevated auditory thresholds and preserved auditory-nerve structures relative to untreated injury. In a mouse model, adding near-infrared PBM to transplanted stem cells increased cell persistence but did not restore auditory responses.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In ouabain-injured gerbils, laser treatment lowered elevated auditory thresholds and preserved auditory-nerve structures relative to untreated injury. In a mouse model, adding near-infrared PBM to transplanted stem cells increased cell persistence but did not restore auditory responses.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Hearing > Auditory neuropathy category contains two unique titles, both from South Korea. They cover different animal approaches rather than clinical cohorts. One study used a gerbil model of ouabain-induced auditory nerve injury. The other used a kanamycin-injured mouse model and combined PBM with transplanted embryonic stem cells. Its cochlear-explant work is an experimental arm of the same publication, not an additional study. No patient study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

No direct human or clinical evidence was identified.

Animal evidence

Lee et al. induced auditory neuropathy in gerbils by locally applying ouabain while sparing the sensory epithelium. Compared with injury alone, 808-nm laser treatment reduced the rise in auditory brainstem response thresholds and preserved spiral ganglion cells, nerve fibers, and synaptic structures (Lee et al. 2016). This is a single induced-animal model and does not show that PBM restores hearing in people.

Chang et al. studied mice with kanamycin-induced secondary auditory nerve degeneration. PBM was given together with transplanted mouse embryonic stem cells. The combination increased persistence of transplanted cells, but auditory brainstem and electrically evoked responses did not recover. One treated animal also showed unusually widespread cell growth, underscoring that the intervention was an exploratory cell-therapy combination rather than PBM alone (Chang et al. 2023).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The 2023 paper included cochlear explants from young mice that were injured with kanamycin and co-cultured with labelled stem cells to observe attachment and integration. This ex-vivo assay did not establish functional hearing recovery and is not an independent PBM experiment or a third publication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The gerbil study used an 808-nm near-infrared laser and reports 200 mW, 0.909 W/cm², 720 J, 3,272 J/cm², a 0.22-cm² treatment area, and a 3,600-second exposure. In the mouse study, an 808-nm near-infrared diode laser irradiated the cochlea through the tympanic membrane for five days after stem-cell transplantation; the database records 0.040 W/cm² and 3,600 seconds. These localized, invasive animal procedures and the cell-therapy combination differ substantially from noninvasive human treatment.

Interpretation

The gerbil experiment reports functional recovery in one induced model, while the later mouse combination study did not restore auditory responses. Because the models and interventions differ and no human evidence exists, the findings establish neither PBM-alone efficacy nor clinical hearing benefit.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for functional auditory recovery in animal models No human evidence identified
Publications and records2 unique titles in Hearing > Auditory neuropathy.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Only two preclinical publications were found. One gerbil study reported functional and histological improvement after 808-nm laser treatment, whereas a mouse study combined PBM with stem-cell transplantation and did not restore hearing. No independent replication or patient trial exists. Replication should test PBM alone, prespecified auditory outcomes, safety, and dosing across models before any human efficacy judgment.
